Thiamin, Riboflavin, and Niacin Thiamin (vitamin B1), riboflavin (vitamin B2), and niacin 
(vitamin B3) function as coenzymes in energy metabolism. This may lead to the notion that require­
ments for these vitamins diminish with declining energy requirements in older adults. However, 
available evidence suggests that requirements for these nutrients are unchanged with age. Potential 
causes of low blood levels include chronic alcohol use (thiamin) and low consumption of dairy 
products (riboflavin). Older patients with food insecurity have been reported to have low intake 
levels of B vitamins.
Folate The RDA for folate in men and women 51 years and older is 400 μg/day. The tolerable upper 
intake limit for folate has been set at 1000 μg/day. Requirements for folate do not change with age; 
however, inadequate folate status contributes to hyperhomocysteinemia, which may increase the 
risk of coronary disease and other chronic diseases common in older adults. Folic acid supplemen­
tation has not been shown to reduce the risk of coronary events. A reduction in stroke events was
